# Fixed parity face witnesses and all-circuit protecting cones
which critical circuits are selected. In a stated regular signed
variation space, it gives an all-circuit gradient rank bound
2^n-1. It does not establish the OC depth constant.

The polar-cone reformulation itself is equivalent to the archived
rainbow condition. The new step is a FIXED witness set of at most
the occupied parity count, selected before any circuits. Ordinary
projected-cover compression may select different anchors after
different circuit choices; that alone would not give this result.

## 1. A fixed face cover of a complete finite lattice set

Let I be a nonempty finite subset of Z^n satisfying

    I=conv(I) intersect Z^n.

Write B=conv(I). For p in I, let F(p) be the minimal face of B
containing p; thus p belongs to relint F(p). This includes B
itself and singleton vertex faces. Let F_1,...,F_s be all the
distinct inclusion-maximal members of the finite family
{F(p):p in I}. Choose a witness p_i with F(p_i)=F_i.
Let k(I) be the number of parity classes occupied by I.

**Lemma 1.**

    I subset union_i F_i,             s<=k(I)<=2^n.       (1)

The witnesses can be fixed from I alone, independently of any
halfspaces or circuits.

**Proof.** Every F(p) is contained in some maximal member of
the finite family, proving coverage.

For any p,q in B, the minimal face of their strict midpoint
m=(p+q)/2 is the smallest face containing both F(p) and F(q).
Indeed a face containing m contains both endpoints of the
segment, hence their minimal faces. Conversely any face
containing both endpoints contains m.

If two distinct witnesses p_i,p_j had the same parity, m would
be an integer point of B, hence belong to I. Its minimal face
would contain both F_i and F_j. These two distinct maximal
members are incomparable, so their join strictly contains
each, contradicting maximality. The witnesses therefore
have distinct parity classes. This proves (1).

No midpoint-component closedness is assumed. Only the
completeness of I and one integer midpoint are used.
The maximal faces can overlap on proper faces, including at
integer points. They are a cover, not a partition.

The bound 2^n is sharp for I={0,1}^n: every point is a vertex,
so all 2^n singleton faces are maximal. If I has a point in
relint B, there is just one maximal face, namely B itself.

## 2. The deepest integer bases form a complete lattice set

Let C be a convex body, d>=1, with positive total mixed
d-volume M. Let P be its finite set of POSITIVE-d-volume
integer bases, and write K_p=C_p for p in P. Other original
fibers may be nonempty and have zero d-volume.

The positive base set P is lattice-complete: at an integer
convex combination of positive bases, the corresponding
Minkowski combination of their positive fibers has positive
d-volume and is contained in the actual section. In
particular any zero-volume original base lies outside
conv(P). A strictly separating pure-integer halfspace
contains its entire fiber and excludes every positive
base, so every point of that zero-volume fiber has depth
zero. Such fibers therefore do not affect the positive
maximum depth or any cap mass.

The canonical hull of the positive fibers has exactly K_p
as its section at every p in P: it is contained in C and
contains each K_p. It may be used for the positive-fiber
geometry below without changing mu or its positive-depth
maximizers. Use mixed d-volume mu, and write Q>0 for the
maximum raw halfspace depth on the actual mixed set S.
Let

    I={p: some (p,x) in S has raw depth Q}.

This set is finite and nonempty. Depth attains its maximum:
its upper level sets are closed, since an outward epsilon
shift of a containing closed halfspace contains every nearby
point, and its measures decrease to the original closed-cap
measure as epsilon decreases to zero. The mixed set is compact.
An interior ball in any positive fiber gives a positive-depth
candidate, so Q>0.

**Lemma 2.** I is lattice-complete in its convex hull.

**Proof.** The depth superlevel set {depth>=Q} in the whole
ambient space is convex. Any halfspace containing a convex
combination of finitely many points must contain at least
one of those points; if they all have depth at least Q,
that halfspace has mass at least Q.

If q in conv(I) is integer, choose deepest points over bases
in a convex representation of q. Their corresponding convex
combination belongs to C and has base q, so it belongs to S.
It has depth at least Q by the preceding argument and hence
exactly Q by maximality. Thus q belongs to I.

This proof does not assert that all points of C are measured
or replace the selected point by a noninteger point.

### Interior anchors and critical contact

Every positive-depth point of an actual full-dimensional
fiber is in its interior. Here is the boundary argument.
Let F be the minimal face of conv(P) containing its base p.
The hull of the fibers above F has dimension dim(F)+d.
A boundary point of K_p is a relative boundary point of this
face body. A supporting normal there has nonzero continuous
component: a purely base functional supporting at p in
relint F would be zero on the entire relative direction
space, contrary to being a nonzero supporting normal.
The outward supporting cap consequently has zero d-volume
in each F-fiber. Adding a sufficiently large multiple of
an affine exposing functional of F, zero on F and strictly
negative at the finitely many other bases, excludes all
off-F fibers. This gives a closed ambient cap of zero
mixed volume through the boundary point.

Now let H be a critical cap of mass Q whose boundary passes
through an interior deepest point. Its own anchor fiber
has a positive proper section. Such a cap cannot strictly
contain any other deepest point: raising its threshold by
a sufficiently small positive amount retains that other
point but removes a positive-volume strip in the original
anchor fiber, giving a containing cap of mass less than Q.
Therefore EVERY deepest point belongs to the closed
complement of H.

## 3. Every circuit at a witness covers its fixed minimal face

At a deepest base p, choose any positive critical circuit:

    H_j={a_j.z+u_j.x>=b_j},       |u_j|=1,
    mu(H_j)=Q,
    rho_j>0,       sum_j rho_j u_j=0.

All cap planes pass through a deepest point at p. Such
finite circuits exist by the previously proved active-normal
balance and capacity-attainment lemmas in
candidate b989614dc4f86228, Sections 5--6:
the source is an actual finite convex fiber family, d>=1,
all fibers used here have positive d-volume, and the
maximizing anchor is interior to its fiber.
Their existence is not inferred here from a genericity
assumption.

Set

    A=sum_j rho_j a_j,       h=sum_j rho_j b_j.

At the anchor, A.p=h. For any q in I, take a deepest point
(q,x_q). The preceding critical-contact argument gives
each cap margin at that point nonpositive. Summing gives

    A.q-h<=0       for every q in I.                    (2)

Thus the projected group inequality A.z-h>=0 is a supporting
inequality on B=conv(I), whose equality face contains p.
If the functional vanishes identically on aff B, its
equality face is all of B. In either case it contains F(p).

For every z in F(p), the weighted sum of cap margins is
zero for EVERY continuous x. Hence at least one margin
is nonnegative, and the closed caps cover the ENTIRE
continuous plane over z. At deepest points above such z,
each individual margin is actually zero, because all are
nonpositive and their positive weighted sum is zero.

Apply Lemma 1 to the deepest set I and fix its witnesses
p_1,...,p_s. The conclusion is:

**Theorem 3.** ANY choice of one critical circuit at EACH
of these fixed witnesses covers every deepest fiber in
its entire continuous plane. There are s<=k(I)<=2^n
witnesses. All chosen circuits have common contact with
all deepest points over the witness's fixed face F_i.

The face overlaps require no assignment of a point to a
unique owner. Coverage is sufficient, and repeated coverage
does not add cap budgets.

## 4. Exact persistence under quantile adjustment

This fixed cover remains usable under nearby actual bodies
C_t provided C_t converges to C in ambient Hausdorff distance
AND each original positive section (C_t)_p converges in
Hausdorff distance to K_p for p in P. The latter is an
explicit assumption: ambient Hausdorff convergence alone
does not ensure lower continuity of boundary-base sections.
The fixed-P positive-fiber variations used in the archived
quantile arguments satisfy these conditions.

Here is an exact repair if additional integer fibers appear.
All C_t lie in one common bounded region, so only a finite
integer base envelope R is relevant. For r in R outside P,
the original section C_r has d-volume zero (and may be
empty). Every limit of points of (C_t)_r belongs to C_r.
Consequently, for each epsilon>0, the new section is
eventually contained in the epsilon-neighborhood of C_r;
if C_r is empty it is eventually empty. The volumes of
these neighborhoods tend to zero. Hence

    e(t):=sum_(r in R outside P)|(C_t)_r| -> 0.

Every such integer r lies outside conv(P), by completeness
of P. Choose a FIXED pure-integer closed halfspace which
contains r and strictly excludes conv(P). As an ambient
cap it contains the entire r-fiber for every t, and its
mixed mass is at most e(t). These finitely many caps cover
all emerging or originally zero-volume fibers, with budgets
tending to zero. Thus they stay strictly slack relative
to Q>0.

Keep each chosen ambient cap normal and each
rho_j fixed. Let Q_j(t,tau) be its nearby threshold giving
cap mass tau. The anchor's positive proper section makes
cap mass locally strictly decreasing with threshold, so
the local quantile exists and is continuous, including
when other fibers have supporting coincidences. Cap mass
is continuous here: the original positive sections
converge in Hausdorff distance, nonvertical cap boundaries
have zero d-volume there, and all other sections have
total mass bounded by e(t).

Choose the unique nearby common group mass tau_i(t) solving

    sum_j rho_j Q_j(t,tau_i(t))=h_i.                   (3)

The right side remains its original constant. Equation
(3) preserves the ENTIRE projected group halfspace
A_i.z>=h_i, and in particular the fixed face F_i. Thus
every chosen group still covers all planes over F_i.

At each originally nondeep base retain its own local
quantile circuit; its original cap mass is strictly below
Q. There are finitely many such bases, so their mass gaps
remain strict near the original family. The resulting
finite cap cover gives the exact upper comparison

    D(S_t)<=max_i tau_i(t)/M_t                         (4)

for sufficiently small t, after keeping both the original
slack groups and the new pure-integer caps below this
right side. It agrees with beta=Q/M at t=0.
No moved center or new deepest-base classification is
needed: every point in every actual new fiber is covered.

The exact quantile existence and nonsmooth inverse formulas
are proved in circuit-quantile-cover-variation.md.
Equation (3) uses the same construction, now with a fixed
small set of witnesses that works for all circuit choices.

## 5. Protecting cones in a regular signed parameter space

Fix a finite-dimensional vector space E parameterizing an
open neighborhood of the original family in an admissible
variation class satisfying Section 4's convergence
hypotheses. Both signs
of each parameter direction are admissible. Assume that the
relevant total-volume and
selected cap/quantile derivatives are linear functionals
on E. These are derivatives of the FULL mixed measure,
including any emerging fibers; an assumption of merely
vanishing new mass would not justify discarding its
first-order contribution. For example, one may use a
common smooth fixed-P deformation
family and circuits whose cap boundaries have zero facet
measure on all moving boundary pieces.

For each fixed witness p_i let Gamma_i be the nonempty set
of ALL critical-circuit response functionals

    g_(i,C)=tau'_(i,C)-beta M'

which meet these linearity hypotheses on E. At least one
such circuit at each witness is an explicit hypothesis.
No claim that every nonsmooth active circuit meets it is
made. Convex hulls may be taken; compactness is unnecessary
for the rank conclusion below.

At a local minimum in this variation class, (4) gives

    max_i g_i(v)>=0
       for every v in E and every selection g_i in Gamma_i.    (5)

For each i define its protecting cone

    T_i={v in E: g(v)>=0 for EVERY g in Gamma_i}.        (6)

These are closed convex cones. Condition (5) is EXACTLY

    E=union_(i=1)^s T_i.                               (7)

Indeed if a direction is outside every T_i, choose a
negative g_i at every index, contradicting (5); the
converse is immediate. Equivalently, every selection has
zero in its convex hull by strict separation in E*.

The cone formulation (7), by itself, is only a reformulation
of the rainbow condition. The additional force here is
that its labels are the fixed parity-bounded witnesses,
not all potentially many deepest bases or a cover-dependent
subset of them.

In a merely one-sided admissible cone D, replace E in
(5)--(7) by D and intersect the protecting sets with D.
The signed rank conclusion below is not asserted on the
full one-sided cone.

## 6. A parity-bounded common kernel for all circuits

**Theorem 4.** Under Section 5's signed-linearity hypotheses,
there is a nonempty essential subset J of the fixed witnesses
such that

    dim span(union_(i in J) Gamma_i)
           <= |J|-1 <= k(I)-1 <=2^n-1.                 (8)

Consequently the common kernel

    L={v in E: g(v)=0 for every i in J, g in Gamma_i}

has codimension at most k(I)-1. EVERY relevant critical
circuit at EVERY witness in J has exactly the normalized
total-volume derivative on L.

Here is the linear-algebra proof, included to specify all
quantifiers. Nonempty sets X_1,...,X_r admit linearly
independent representatives if and only if

    dim span(union_(i in A)X_i)>=|A|
                                  for every A.         (9)

Necessity is immediate. For sufficiency, if a nonempty
proper A is tight, choose independent representatives
there by induction, and apply induction in the quotient
by their full span for the other indices. The required
quotient dimensions follow by applying (9) to A united
with each remaining subset. If no such subset is tight,
choose a nonzero representative of the last set. Every
nonempty proper remaining subset had dimension at least
its cardinality plus one, so quotienting by that vector
preserves (9). Induction completes the proof.

Now choose J inclusion-minimal with the universal
zero-convex-hull property, and relabel it {1,...,r}.
Every representative system is dependent. By (9) there
is a subset A with positive deficiency

    d(A)=|A|-dim V_A>0,
    V_A=span(union_(i in A)Gamma_i).

Choose A with maximal deficiency. For every subset B
of its complement, maximality gives

    dim(V_A+V_B)-dim V_A>=|B|.

Use (9) in the quotient to choose all outside representatives
linearly independent modulo V_A. For ANY choices inside A,
universal positive dependence gives a probability combination
of all representatives equal to zero. Projection to the
quotient forces every outside coefficient to vanish.
Thus A alone has the universal zero-convex-hull property.
Minimality of J forces A=J, and its positive deficiency
gives (8).

The argument applies to the entire circuit sets at these
witnesses at once; it does not select a separate kernel
for each cover. It does NOT give fixed balancing weights
for all covers. The frozen-weight counterexample and its
singleton criterion remain valid.

## 7. Quantitative cone coverage that counts overlaps correctly

Choose any Euclidean inner product on E of positive dimension
and its standard Gaussian probability measure sigma. Define
omega_i=sigma(T_i). The finite cover (7) gives the exact
overlap identity

    sum_i omega_i
      =1+integral [sum_i 1_(T_i)(v)-1] dsigma(v) >=1.    (10)

In particular at least one protecting cone has

    omega_i>=1/s>=1/k(I)>=2^(-n).                     (11)

No disjointness of the protecting cones is presumed.
Overlaps contribute the nonnegative term in (10), rather
than being silently counted as a partition.

If Gamma_i contains a nonzero functional, T_i lies in a
closed halfspace through zero, hence omega_i<=1/2.
If s=1, (7) therefore forces Gamma_1={0}, directly also
from signed directions. If an essential cover has s=2,
both cones are proper and (10) forces each to have
Gaussian measure exactly 1/2 with null overlap. A closed
convex cone contained in a halfspace and having its full
Gaussian measure equals that halfspace: a missing interior
point would give a missing open neighborhood of positive
measure, and closure supplies the boundary. The two
halfspaces are therefore opposite. The two gradient
families lie on opposite nonnegative rays.

The bound 1/s is sharp for abstract protecting cones:
in a two-dimensional parameter plane take s equally spaced
closed sectors of angle 2pi/s, for any s>=2. They cover
the plane with disjoint interiors and each is the
intersection of two homogeneous halfspaces, hence is
the protecting cone of a two-point gradient set.
Thus cone counting alone cannot improve (11).

These Gaussian probabilities concern directions in the
chosen deformation space, not mixed volume in the original
source. They are a quantitative coverage invariant, not
an OC mass estimate.

## 8. Nonsmooth scope and remaining issue

The FIXED witness construction and exact quantile covers
in Sections 1--4 require no smoothness, fan, or general
position assumption. At a nonsmooth cap coincidence, a
circuit has the exact continuous positively homogeneous
budget response from the archived quantile inverse rule.
The universal condition still says that each admissible
direction has a witness at which every relevant circuit
response is nonnegative.

However its protecting set need not be convex, because
those responses may contain integrated min/max branches.
One must not apply the linear rank theorem to those sets
or interchange prescribed inside allocations with the
outside allocations supplied by separation.

Thus the new general arithmetic conclusion is the fixed
parity-bounded witness set. Its common-kernel consequence
is proved in the explicitly linear signed phase. Neither
conclusion yet supplies a below-target descent direction
or a bound on the original boundary-source mass.
